# Introduction {.unnumbered}

This project focuses on recreating a data visualisation illustrating the relationship between Germany's population development and net migration over time.

The original visualisation was created by Luc Guillemot and uses data from the United Nations. My objective was to reproduce its design using R and ggplot2, while practising more advanced visualisation techniques.

Rather than presenting an original statistical analysis, this project focuses on visual communication: transforming historical data into an informative and visually engaging chart.

The visualisation highlights several historical periods and uses annotations, colour gradients and carefully positioned labels to guide the reader through the data.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggtext)
library(here)
```

# Data and preparation

The dataset contains historical observations of Germany's population and net migration rate.

The first step is to import the dataset and prepare the variables for visualisation. This involves assigning meaningful column names, converting variables to numeric format, removing observations with missing years and adjusting population values to millions where necessary.

The original dataset is stored in the `data` folder within this project.

```{r}
#| label: data-preparation

temp_env <- new.env()

loaded_names <- load(here("data", "germany_migration_data.RData"),
  envir = temp_env
)

my_data <- temp_env[[loaded_names[1]]]

# Rename the first three columns
colnames(my_data)[1:3] <- c("year","population","migration_rate")

# Ensure all variables are stored in numeric format
my_data$year <- as.numeric(my_data$year)
my_data$population <- as.numeric(my_data$population)
my_data$migration_rate <- as.numeric(my_data$migration_rate)

# Remove missing years and arrange observations
my_data <- my_data |>
  filter(!is.na(year)) |>
  arrange(year)

# Convert population to millions where necessary
if (max(my_data$population, na.rm = TRUE) > 1000000) {
  my_data$population <- my_data$population / 1000000
}
```

# Preparing the visual elements

Before constructing the chart, several additional variables are created to control its visual appearance.

First, selected historical periods are identified and displayed in grey. This creates a visual distinction between different periods of Germany's population development.

Second, a set of key years is selected for annotation. These observations are highlighted using larger points and year labels.

Because some labels would otherwise overlap with the data points or other annotations, their positions are adjusted manually using separate horizontal and vertical offsets.

Finally, the minimum and maximum years are identified to ensure that the colour gradient remains consistent across the visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: visual-elements
# Identify historical periods to be displayed in grey
grey_periods <- my_data |> 
  filter(year <= 1952 |
      (year >= 1973 & year <= 1984) |
      (year >= 2000 & year <= 2007)) |> 
  mutate(grey_group = case_when(
      year <= 1952 ~ 1,
      year >= 1973 & year <= 1984 ~ 2,
      year >= 2000 & year <= 2007 ~ 3
    )
  )

# Years that need labels
key_years <- c(1950, 1973, 1980, 1984, 1991, 2000, 2007, 2016, 2022)

labels_data <- my_data |> 
  filter(year %in% key_years) |> 
  mutate(
    move_x = case_when(
      year == 1950 ~ 0.45,
      year == 1984 ~ -0.35,
      year == 1973 ~ 0.35,
      year == 2007 ~ -0.35,
      year == 2000 ~ 0.35,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    move_y = case_when(
      year == 1950 ~ 0,
      year == 1973 ~ -0.1,
      year == 1980 ~ -0.5,
      year == 1984 ~ 0,
      year == 1991 ~ 0.5,
      year == 2000 ~ 0,
      year == 2007 ~ 0,
      year == 2016 ~ 0.5,
      year == 2022 ~ -0.5,
      TRUE ~ 0.35
    )
  )

# Identify highlighted years that will use grey markers
grey_highlight_years <- c(1950, 1980, 2000, 2007)

# keep the same year colours for the whole graph
min_yr <- min(my_data$year)
max_yr <- max(my_data$year)

```

# Building the visualisation

The visualisation is constructed using ggplot2, with population on the horizontal axis and net migration rate on the vertical axis.

Several graphical layers are combined to create the final chart.

The main trajectory is represented by a path whose colour changes over time, using a gradient from yellow to orange and pink. Selected historical periods are overlaid in grey to create visual contrast.

Additional layers highlight important observations, add year labels and provide contextual annotations explaining different stages of Germany's population development.

The chart also includes custom axis scales, descriptive labels and a minimalist theme to improve readability.

```{r}
#| label: build-visualisation

# Initialise the plot using population and net migration data
final_plot <- ggplot(
  my_data, aes(x = population, y = migration_rate)) +

# Add a reference line at zero to distinguish positive and negative net migration
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +

# Draw the main trajectory, with colour representing the year
  geom_path(aes(color = year), linewidth = 2.5, alpha = 0.35) +

# Highlight selected historical periods in grey
  geom_path(data = grey_periods, aes(group = grey_group),
    color = "grey65",linewidth = 2.5) +

  # Add points representing individual yearly observations
  geom_point(aes(color = year),size = 1.2) +

  # Display observations from the highlighted periods in grey
  geom_point(data = grey_periods, color = "grey55", size = 1.25) +

  # Highlight selected years with larger circular markers
  geom_point(data = filter(labels_data, !year %in% grey_highlight_years),
    aes(fill = year),
    shape = 21,
    color = "black",
    size = 2.2,
    stroke = 0.6
  ) +

  # Use grey markers for selected years within the highlighted periods
  geom_point(
    data = filter(labels_data, year %in% grey_highlight_years),
    fill = "grey55", shape = 21, color = "black", size = 2.2, stroke = 0.6) +

  # Add year labels with manually adjusted positions
  geom_text(
    data = labels_data,
    aes(x = population + move_x, y = migration_rate + move_y, label = year),
    size = 3.2, fontface = "bold", color = "#222222") +

  # Apply a yellow-to-pink colour gradient to represent the progression of time
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = c("#f6d258", "#e27442", "#c2335b"),
    limits = c(min_yr, max_yr),
    guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = c("#f6d258", "#e27442", "#c2335b"),
    limits = c(min_yr, max_yr),
    guide = "none") +

  # Set axis breaks, limits and labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(69, 84, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "M"),
    limits = c(68, 84.5),
    expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-12, 10, by = 2),
    limits = c(-12.5, 10.5),
    expand = c(0, 0)) +

  # Add the title, subtitle and source information
  labs(
    title = "Germany's population growth has been driven by immigration",
    subtitle = paste(
      "In the postwar era, Germany has experienced three periods",
      "of population growth. Only the first was significantly driven by births."
    ),
    x = "",
    y = "",
    caption = paste0(
      "Population based on Germany's current borders<br>",
      "Chart: Luc Guillemot • Source: United Nations"
    )) +

  # Add labels identifying population and net migration
  annotate("text", x = 68.1, y = 10, label = "Net migration rate",
    fontface = "bold", hjust = 0,
    size = 3.3, color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 84.3, y = -12, label = "Total population",
    fontface = "bold", hjust = 1, size = 3.3, color = "grey40") +

  # Explain the meaning of positive and negative net migration
  annotate("text", x = 68.1, y = 1.5, 
    label = "▲\nMore immigration\nthan emigration",
    size = 3, hjust = 0, color = "#555555") +
  annotate("text", x = 68.1, y = -1.5,
    label = "More emigration\nthan immigration\n▼",
    size = 3, hjust = 0, color = "#555555") +

  # Indicate the direction of time along the trajectory
  annotate("richtext", x = 71.3, y = -4.5, 
    label = "**Time follows<br>the line**",size = 3, hjust = 0,
    fill = NA, label.color = NA) +
  annotate("point", x = 71.3, y = -3.9, shape = 17, size = 1.2) +

  # Annotate the increase in immigration after World War II
  annotate("richtext", x = 69.5, y = -7.5,
    label = "Immigration<br>increases<br>dramatically<br>post WWII",
    size = 3, hjust = 0.5, color = "#555555", fill = NA, label.color = NA) +
  annotate("segment", x = 70.3, y = -7.5, xend = 70.9, yend = -7.5,
    color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3) +

  # Add historical context for population growth during the economic miracle
  annotate("richtext", x = 72, y = 5.5,
    label = paste0(
      "During the \"economic miracle,\" millions of<br>",
      "**guest workers** come to Germany.<br>",
      "The **fertility rate is also still high**, which explains<br>",
      "this dramatic population growth."),
    size = 3, hjust = 0, color = "#555555",fill = NA, label.color = NA) +

  annotate("segment", x = 73, y = 4,
    xend = 73, yend = 1.5, color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3) +

  # Explain the decline between 1973 and 1980 and the subsequent policy changes
  annotate("richtext", x = 78.5, y = -5,
    label = paste0(
      "Between 1973 and 1980, the world is in crisis.<br>",
      "Immigration slows and the population declines.<br>",
      "In the 1970s, Germany passes **family reunification**<br>",
      "**laws**, which help to restart immigration."),
    size = 3, hjust = 0.5,
    color = "#555555", fill = NA, label.color = NA) +

  annotate("segment", x = 78.5, y = -3.5,
    xend = 78.5, yend = -0.5, color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3) +

  # Annotate renewed population growth before German reunification
  annotate("richtext", x = 78, y = 8.5,
    label = paste0(
      "Immigration drives renewed<br>",
      "population growth in the<br>",
      "years leading up to<br>",
      "German reunification."),
    size = 3, hjust = 0.5,
    color = "#555555",
    fill = NA, label.color = NA) +

  annotate("segment", x = 78, y = 7.2, xend = 78, yend = 5.5,
    color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3) +

  # Explain migration-related population growth following EU enlargement
  annotate("richtext", x = 81.5, y = 8.5,
    label = paste0(
      "After the **expansion of the EU** in the 2000s,<br>",
      "many Eastern Europeans migrate to Germany,<br>",
      "mainly from Poland and Romania."),
    size = 3, hjust = 0.5,
    color = "#555555", fill = NA, label.color = NA) +

  annotate("segment", x = 81.5, y = 7.2,
    xend = 81.5, yend = 4.5,color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3) +

  # Apply the final theme and adjust the appearance of the chart
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 17, face = "bold",
      margin = margin(b = 6)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11.5,
      margin = margin(b = 20)
    ),
    plot.caption = element_markdown(
      hjust = 0,
      lineheight = 1.5,
      margin = margin(t = 18)
    ),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )
```

# Final visualisation

The final chart combines the population trajectory, migration patterns, historical highlights and explanatory annotations.

The result is an editorial-style visualisation designed to guide the reader through the relationship between population development and migration over time.

```{r}
#| label: final-chart
#| fig-width: 12.4
#| fig-height: 8.8

final_plot

```

# Exporting the visualisation

The final visualisation is exported as a high-resolution PNG image. This allows it to be viewed independently of the R environment and included in other project documentation.

```{r}
#| label: export-chart
#| include: false

ggsave(
  filename = here("figures", "germany_migration.png"),
  plot = final_plot,
  width = 12.4,
  height = 8.8,
  dpi = 200,
  units = "in",
  bg = "white"
)
```

# What I learned

This project allowed me to practise several advanced ggplot2 techniques and explore how detailed visual design can improve data communication.

In particular, I worked with:

- Layered visualisations using `geom_path()`, `geom_point()` and `geom_text()`.
- Continuous colour gradients to represent time.
- Custom annotations and manually positioned labels.
- Separately highlighting specific observations and historical periods.
- Advanced theme customisation and formatting using ggplot2 and ggtext.

One of the main challenges was balancing the amount of information displayed in the chart while maintaining readability.

This exercise also demonstrated how visualisation choices can guide the interpretation of historical data.
